utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow me in a language that -- can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Anna Richterova, Sureta Chana assisted by Hasan Younis case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you madam, and good morning to the three of you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm John Ackerman. I'm here today with Vesna Anic who is assisting me today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you both. So before we bring in the witness, is there anything that you would like to tell the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we have major problems with yesterday's events, Your Honour. I don't know who can be with me in court tomorrow. I have not arranged for anybody to be with me in court tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am inquiring myself about that, to make sure that you are assisted, and if you are not assisted, then obviously we won't be able to sit. It's as simple as that. Until the situation is -- clears up. As far as today is concerned, as you know, when I was informed yesterday afternoon, I agreed to the postponement of the sitting until I could -- I had a guarantee that you would be assisted. Of course I consulted with my two colleagues and the position is that I don't know what the situation is going to be tomorrow as yet but I have got someone working on it who should be informing me in a question of minutes because he was working on it before the sitting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wasn't able to reach Mr. Roberts last night. It's possible that he will be available tomorrow afternoon and if he's not available, then I will talk to Ms. Anic to see if she is available tomorrow afternoon. I don't know if she is. She is. So we can cover tomorrow afternoon one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's one thing. Unless -- I'm just thinking aloud, unless you prefer, if it is possible, I don't know if it is possible at all, to finish today, which would entail going into the afternoon. In other words, stopping at quarter to 2.00, then resuming again at quarter past 2.00 and provided we can finish by half past 4.00, we could possibly conclude today rather than go into tomorrow. But I am not quite sure whether that is okay with -- because everyone has to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's really not possible because of preparation with Mr. Brdjanin for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then forget about it. Okay. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No time to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just made the suggestion -- we were talking about it outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I appreciate you suggesting that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will see whether there is agreement on this. Yes, Mr. Ackerman, I know that the Registrar's office is looking into your problems, your client's problems. Hopefully you will find a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The registry of course has been informed of the situation Your Honour. Mr. Brdjanin would like to speak with Ms. Jevtovic. She came here yesterday, paid her own way here, just for the purpose of telling me what her position was. Since I've told the registry that she has left the case I don't know if she'll have trouble getting into the detention centre to speak with Mr. Brdjanin or not but I think it's important that that happen because that could make a favourable change in the situation. So if I need your assistance with regard to that, I may ask you this afternoon for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, actually, we -- I have absolutely -- as a trial judge, neither I nor my two colleagues, nor as a Trial Chamber, I don't think we do have the jurisdiction to interfere into what is absolutely the discretionary in the hands of the commandant of the detention unit. However, I also can assure you that the commandant of the detention unit is a very reasonable --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He would not interfere at all, Your Honour, it would be the registry that would not authorise her, Ms. Martinez, and if Ms. Martinez authorises her to visit then there is no problem. She's currently authorised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How can Ms. Martinez authorise Ms. Jevtovic to visit the detention centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the way it works, that's the way it works. Nobody is allowed to visit the detention centre until OLAD authorises it from a Defence standpoint --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if she is no longer on the Defence team Ms. Martinez doesn't come into the picture at all. It's just like any other ordinary person that would like to pay a visit to one of the detainees over there and I don't think that in that case, you go do the Registrar or you go through the Registrar but not through --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will talk to Ms. Martinez and find out what her final position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, Madam Chuqing can forward this part of the transcript to both Ms. Martinez and Mr. McFadden, that we've taken into consideration the suggestion of Mr. Ackerman that an interview between Ms. -- Madam Marela Jevtovic and the accused could be useful at this point in time, and that we recommend that this -- such a meeting is facilitated. Beyond that, I don't think we can go because it does not depend on us, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So a copy of this part of the transcript, Madam Jevtovic, goes to Ms. Martinez, as far as she may have jurisdiction now or may not have jurisdiction, I don't know. The Registrar for all intents and purposes, Mr. McFadden. Thank you. So let's bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Doslic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask you to make the solemn declaration -- repeat your solemn declaration again, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Ackerman who is representing Mr. Brdjanin will start with his cross-examination. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you cross that bridge in Donji Vakuf and drive for about 12 kilometres, you come to Bugojno, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in April and May of 1992, Bugojno was a 100 per cent -- virtually 100 per cent Muslim city, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Confrontation line between HVO, Muslim and Serb forces was very near to Donji Vakuf, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In May, there were no lines at all. Not in that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: People who left Donji Vakuf in May went to Bugojno because that was a Muslim-controlled area and a safe haven for them, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People left Bugojno for the territory and went their separate ways, throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But people left Donji Vakuf and went to Bugojno, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, not everyone was leaving Donji Vakuf. People left in waves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question was not whether everyone left or not. My question was people left Bugojno -- people left Donji Vakuf and went to Bugojno, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't ask you if everyone did. I said people left Donji Vakuf and went to Bugojno, didn't they? Some people.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The bridge that was blown up in Donji Vakuf, you know, do you not, that there was a truck with coal in it that contained explosives that exploded and blew up the bridge?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard, and I also saw the remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You saw coal lying around the bridge area, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, you named some people who you knew that were killed in this explosion. Could you tell us again what those people's names were?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one was a barber, Safet. There was a waiter who had worked in a cafe near the bridge by the name of Cikota, and there was a child whose name I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know the ethnicity of any of these people?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at document now P1750, would you please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was used yesterday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, you looked at this yesterday and I'm just going to refer you back to a section that you saw yesterday. It's -- I don't know how it looks in your version but part way through, several paragraphs down, there is a paragraph that says, "It all started on April 30 when Croats and Muslims from neighbouring towns sent us a lorry full of explosives hidden under a load of coal, Ninkovic said." As far as you know, this is a correct account, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at an Exhibit P899 now, please. This is a document, sir, dated 5 May, 1992. This would be, if the bridge were destroyed on April 30th, this would be like five days later. You'll notice that it's a document from the 5th Corps command, Major General Momir Talic addressed to the 30th Partisan Brigade command and signed by someone on behalf of Major General Talic, and it says this: "Since the bridge in Donji Vakuf and the transmitter in the wider area of Kljuc have recently been destroyed in your zone of responsibility, and you did not have a valid assessment regarding the securing of the vital facilities in your area of responsibility, I order, number 1, that you send me an assessment of all the vital facilities in your zone of responsibility and the forces with which you are securing them." Now, would you agree that General Talic is criticising the 30th Partisan Brigade for not protecting that bridge and telling them that he immediately wants a report from them on all the other vital facilities and how they are going to protect them?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at number 2. He says, "Submit a detailed report on the aim of the demonstration of Serbian extremism in Kljuc and Donji Vakuf and to what degree it was initiated by official organs." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what demonstration of Serbian extremism went on in Donji Vakuf in early May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the bridge was blown up, the strength of military formations and units increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You actually heard, didn't you, that that bridge was blown up by Croats?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look, please, and the Prosecution will provide you with this, a statement that you gave on 23 August, 1994, before the investigating judge of the High Court in Zenica. First thing I'd like you to do, sir, is look at the last page of that report and tell me if it bears your signature.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, it's on page 3 in the English version, I'm not sure where it is in your version but please find a paragraph that begins with the language, "We watched from Donji Vakuf as the Serbs with the then Yugoslav army" and so forth. Tell me when you find that paragraph. "We watched from Donji Vakuf." Have you found that paragraph yet?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look a little ways down in that paragraph, sir, I think you will find this language: "I think the Croats pulled down the bridge on the Vrbas River on 30 April, 1992, around 0500 hours, which provided the motive for the Serbs to begin their terror." You see that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was a statement you made in -- on the 23rd of August, 1994, a little more than two years after these events, correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that you signed your name to?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. But it was never established who blew up the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why he says I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that's why you say I think. The question I asked you earlier was you heard that the bridge was blown up by Croats, didn't you, you said no. But in this statement you say you think it was pulled down by Croats, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how it was at the beginning but it was later revealed that no one knows who the perpetrator was, so I can't say anything one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, in your testimony here, LiveNote page 12 and 13, you said that you had heard the explosion and saw the smoke from the destruction of this bridge, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told us that you were nearby in the company of your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told us that it happened in the afternoon. That's what you told us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In 1994, in August, when you talked to the judge of the High Court, you told him that it happened on 30 April, 1992, around 0500 hours, 5.00 in the morning. I just want to know what caused you to change your story between 1994 and yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That did not happen in the morning, because it says 5.00 here and 5.00 can also be in the afternoon, because we write 5.00 as 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This says 0500 hours, doesn't it? Or is it a translation problem?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you signed it. You don't know who wrote it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. In our language, you can write 5, and it can mean both a.m. and p.m. I don't know how you do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I have another document I'd like you to look at. It's disclosure number 4.1552, 136?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Your Honour I'll mark that as DB136. Your Honour, I must tell you that I have extracted just two pages to make this exhibit from a very long document that -- I'm sorry? It's only in English. I only have an English version so if you put it on the ELMO, a very long document, I don't have the B/C/S version of the document, it's a notebook from the 5th Krajina Corps, that's how it's described in the disclosure to me. It's some kind of a daily record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I don't have a version of this in your language so all I can do is read to you from page 108 of this document. You understand that it's represented as a notebook that came from the 5th Krajina Corps. At page 108 of that document the following entry appears: Under number 2. "At 1740 hours, on 30 April, the bridge in Donji Vakuf was destroyed. At that moment, a cargo truck came along carrying coal from Gracanica. Instead of coal the truck contained large quantities of explosives. It blew up, destroying the bridge. Besides the bridge, which cannot be used, several houses were destroyed. There were casualties as well as material damage, large number of dead and wounded, seven killed [four children] and 20 injured. Driver captured, Croat from Livno." See that? You don't see it but you heard the translation, correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to doubt that report?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know and I never heard anything about a driver being captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you now to just -- there is another page to that document. You know, do you not, that that bridge was rather speedily restored by the JNA? In fact it was restored just four days later, I think on May 5th. Do you know that to be the case?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did repair the bridge. I don't know the date, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you just look at the next page of that document, page 113, there is an entry that says, "The bridge was set up in Donji Vakuf at 1600 hours," and I believe the date of that entry is 4 or 5 May, 1992. Now, I think you told us yesterday that you couldn't think of any reason why the Croats would blow up that bridge. Isn't it the case that the Croats would blow up that bridge to try to prevent Serb forces from crossing the Vrbas River into what was Muslim-Croat territory?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know there were units of the 5th Krajina Corps stationed in the area of Donji Vakuf, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whose corps was there at the time. All I know is that there were troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at another statement you made on 15 January, 1993. This was to state security detachment in Bugojno. And again what I'd like you to do is look at the very last page and see if you see your signature there.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is a statement that you gave January 15, 1993, less than a year after the events of May, 1992. If you look at the next to the last paragraph of this document, you say this: "I would also like to add that a part of the Banja Luka Corps with heavy artillery is stationed in the area of Donji Vakuf." Does that refresh your recollection as to what it was you knew at that time in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. Does that statement that you made in 1993 refresh your recollection as to what it was you knew at that time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the way it says in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday, you named some persons who would come to the camps, both the TO warehouse and Vrbaspromet and beat people. Some of the names you mentioned were Jordan Ilic, Vojo Jandric, a person called Balaban, Brane Pacavra, Sasa Krivosija and some others. You referred to them as soldiers. Did you call them soldiers because they were wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They were not members of any regular army unit that you know of, were they?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they wore emblems, arm bands, with writing on them in Cyrillic that said "police."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were they wearing blue uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue and brown. Camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If they were police, they were not soldiers, then, were they? Or do you make a distinction?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Brane Pacavra had a uniform with a white belt, and an olive green grey uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Any conclusion you make about whether they were part of any organised unit is based solely upon your observation of their uniforms, and you have no other information regarding that, do you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you that they wore blue and brown camouflage uniforms. Two or three among them, including Pacavra and Satara had such uniforms with white belts. The colour of their uniforms was olive green grey. The people who were with me, such as Vojo Ilic, who used to work with me, suddenly became a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you about Jordan Ilic. What kind of a uniform did you see him wearing?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He too wore the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Which?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did he have a blue uniform?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any idea who it was, what unit?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue and brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, do you have any idea what unit it was that he was part of, who was his commander, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a policeman who brought people in and beat them, and everybody addressed the warden of this prison of -- or whatever you want to call it, Djurkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go to another subject. You spoke yesterday of a person named Novo Boroja and how he treated you very well. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Judges the things it was that he did to help you and treat you well?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we used to be neighbours, we knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question is tell the Judges the things he did to help you and treat you well. What specifically did he do to help you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, he almost saved my life on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Like when the old woman tried to stab you with her sword?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was the other occasion?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second occasion was when we were building a stable and one man wanted to cut my head off with an axe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Novo Boroja prevented that, did he?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you hinted at least yesterday that he assisted you with food.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What other assistance? Can you think of any other assistance he gave you, anything else he did to help you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, sometimes when he had time to spare, he would come to my house and we would sit up until the small hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's your position that he helped you because you were neighbours and friends, correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume he's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at a document P1706, please. Sir, if you look at the second page of that document, I assume it's the second page, you'll see a list of 30 people and then three more that are handwritten, that are people who were appointed to be members of the assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Donji Vakuf. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These three men down below.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Turn the page. There are 30. The next page. See the long list of names?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you about three of those people. Number 3 is Ilija Boroja. Number 4 is Ranko Boroja?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And number 30 is Zeljko Boroja. Can you tell us if any of those people are related to Novo Boroja?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly whether they are related. I know that Ilija Boroja -- I know Ilija Boroja very well. As to whether they were related, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Serbs in Donji Vakuf certainly were aware that Novo Boroja was helping you and assisting you, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Wouldn't people have learned on those two occasions at least that he tried to save your life and actually succeeded in saving your life, that he was helping you, protecting you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I have to say that this man helped me a lot. Whether he was related with them, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question has to do with other Serbs in Donji Vakuf being aware that he was in fact protecting and assisting you. They would have had to have been aware of that, at least some of them, correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of the three of them, no, they didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know where Novo Boroja is today?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have reliable information but I did inquire through these people, and I heard that he spent sometime in Banja Luka, sometime in Gradiska but I don't know his exact whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to talk to you for a moment now about work obligations because you talked about being released from Vrbaspromet and assigned to a work obligation. Do you know that in the event of a mobilisation, that persons mobilised must either go into a military unit or can, under certain conditions, perform a work obligation as a substitute for going into a military unit? Do you know that that's the case, that that was the law?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that if you have a work obligation, a certified work obligation, then you're exempted from going into the military and going to fight at the front line, for instance?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a compulsory obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Any time there is a mobilisation and people are called up, that's a compulsory obligation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not in this case. It was not an obligation in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, don't you, that there were Serbs in Donji Vakuf who were mobilised and did not go into the military but instead were performing work obligations as a substitute? You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of them were in some sort of military service, and all detainees and others were performing work obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But my question was, you also know that there were Serbs in Donji Vakuf who were mobilised and performing work obligations, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to go back to this statement that you made to the judge at the High Court of Zenica on August 23rd, 1994. You still have that? I want to refer you to the third paragraph of your statement, sir. It begins with the language, "The first accused Nedeljko Ninkovic." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, according to this, you also said the following with regard to the SDS: "Within the framework of the parties activities, he, meaning Nedeljko Ninkovic, received orders from higher levels of decision making that were then, as now, headed by Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Nikola Koljevic, Biljana Plavsic and other criminals, who in their turn may have been receiving orders and guidelines for this monstrous policy from their leadership in Serbia." Now, where did you come up with that information? Did Nedeljko Ninkovic tell you that he was getting orders from Karadzic and Krajisnik and Koljevic and Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where did you come up with this information? What caused to you say that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What caused me to say this was my experience and my suffering. This is what I experienced on my own skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You experienced Nedeljko Ninkovic receiving orders from higher levels on your own skin?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who he received his orders from. I just told them my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, no where in there does it say that it's your opinion. You represent this in this statement as something you know. So it's the case that you really don't know any of the things you say in that paragraph that it's just your opinion, your guess, correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here, "I personally know." And once again, this was my personal opinion, my personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says you personally know Nedeljko Ninkovic but you just told us that he didn't tell you any of these things, correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me anything but I know him because he used to be my teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me suggest to you, sir, this: That someone else wrote this in your statement, that these are not your words, and that you didn't actually say this, you just adopted it. Isn't that true? Isn't that what really happened?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What exactly do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have in mind --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What really happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have in mind that someone else put this in the statement, that these are not really your words.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These are my words and my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So you want us to believe that on that date, in August of 1994, you said, "Within the framework of the party's activities, he, meaning Nedeljko Ninkovic, received orders from higher levels of decision making that were then, as now, headed by Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Nikola Koljevic, Biljana Plavsic and other criminals, who in their turn may have been receiving orders and guidelines for this monstrous policy from their leadership in Serbia"? You're telling us that those are your words, that that's what you said? Correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I stated and these are my personal words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell us what information you had at your disposal on that date that caused you to arrive at this opinion? What did you know?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, I told you that this was my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But what did you know that let you make this opinion? I mean, you have to have some facts to draw an opinion, to make an opinion, don't you? What facts did you have? What did you know?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that Nedeljko Ninkovic was the SDS leader in Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A little further on in this document, sir, it's over on page 4 of the English version, in this statement, I want you to look for a paragraph that begins with, "I was enjoying some sort of freedom." It's probably two pages after what you just saw. It begins with the language, "I was enjoying some sort of freedom."

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what this says, according to my translation, "I was enjoying some sort of freedom in Donji Vakuf until Stamenko Satara and Jordan Ilic arrested me for no reason on 16 June, 1992." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said that in a statement that you signed your name to, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look now at the statement you made on 15 January, 1993, again a statement that you signed --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this is about seven months after you were actually arrested. What you told state security in Bugojno on 15 January, 1993, was this, and you'll find this in the one, two, three, fourth paragraph after the word "statement." "I can say without a doubt that it was precisely because I had been denounced by Celic that I was arrested." That's what you said on 15 January, 1993. And then by August of 1994, you were arrested for no reason?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman I have to stop you here because three lines further down he also says in the same statement, "I'm not familiar with the real reasons behind my arrest."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but he says he can say without doubt that it was precisely because he'd been denounced by Celic. That's the statement I'm dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, but you need to point that out to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what you said, wasn't it, "I can say without a doubt that it was precisely because I had been denounced by Celic that I was arrested"?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Halil Celic is my neighbour who went around with them and he pointed to the houses where the people lived, and he collaborated with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, but my question is not that. My question is: Did you say this: "I can say without a doubt that it was precisely because I had been denounced by Celic that I was arrested"? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what it says. What it says here is what I actually told them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you read -- could you read your version and so I can hear the translation of it? Start with, "Furthermore Celic went around Muslim houses." Just read that entire paragraph to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And before -- one moment, before he does that, please, the interpreters that will be translating into English, just make sure that you interpret what he will be reading and not what is contained already in the English translation of the same document that we have, because it's important to know exactly what at this present moment you consider to be the correct interpretation of what is contained in this particular part of the statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, read that whole paragraph that begins with "Furthermore Celic" and read it very slowly so that the interpreters can interpret it for us.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Together with the members of the above mentioned military police, Celic went around Muslim houses and searched them together with them. I can claim, I can freely claim that it was precisely because I had been denounced by Celic that I was arrested, as was the case with Nasko Dosic and our neighbours, Esad Becar, Abdulah Began, Smajo Rahmanovic, and Hamid Rahmanovic. The real reasons behind my arrest are not familiar to me." And then the date here, the 17th of June is not correct. It happened on the 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You'll concede that what you have just read to us is in fact what you said?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was what you said on 15 January, 1993, very shortly after the events, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you say in connection with saying precisely you were arrested because you'd been denounced by Celic and then you follow that with I'm not familiar with the real reasons, I take it what you mean is you knew that he had denounced you and caused your arrest but you didn't know what it was he had said about you, the reasons that he had given?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. May I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. May I explain, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Halil Celic, as I have already said, collaborated with them, since Brane Pacavra and Satara, whose name I don't know, are not from Donji Vakuf, they didn't know who lived where, and where their houses were. So it was him who told them who lived where and which house belonged to whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you have no idea what Celic told them about you, do you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at P1750 now, sir. You saw this yesterday, we'll look at it again now. I'm sorry, that's the wrong number, Your Honour. It's 1759. Yesterday, you found your name in that document. I think you'll find it on page 8, sir. You'll recall that this document says that you were arrested because you were suspected of possession of weapons, correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is what it says, isn't it? It says you were arrested because you were suspected of possession of weapons. That's what the document says, correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a Serbian document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. I'm just asking you if that's what it says. It says you were arrested on 16 June, 1992, and that you were suspected of possession of weapons?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm only asking you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If that's what it says. That's what it says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now it may very well be, since you have no idea what it was that Celic told the police about that, that he told them that you had weapons Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 14915 to 14918. and that they therefore suspected that you had weapons and that's why they arrested you.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had any weapons, nor do I have any weapons today, nor does any member of my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am not suggesting that you had weapons.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that you had weapons. I'm suggesting that this Celic, who was denouncing everybody, may very well have told the police that you had weapons.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't know that he didn't?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But after a period of time, in confinement, during which time you were never beaten, you were then released, apparently because there was no evidence developed that you ever possessed weapons, correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why they released me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't know of your own personal knowledge who it was that destroyed any of the mosques in Donji Vakuf, do you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Donji Vakuf, when the mosque was destroyed, there were no more than 50 Muslims left, women, children, and elderly. There were only Serbs left. So who else could have destroyed it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're misunderstanding my question. The question is quite simple. You don't know of your own personal knowledge who it was that destroyed the mosques in Donji Vakuf, do you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first mosque you talked about yesterday, I think it's called the Dudica Dzamija?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you told us that that was basically a wooden structure with the exception of the -- of parts of it, and it burned down?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Novo Boroja told you that it had been set on fire, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday, LiveNote 37, page 37, line 17, you were asked this question, from line 16: "Were you ever informed as to this fire and the cause of it?" And you gave this answer: "Well, we learned that either Serb policemen or Serb soldiers had set it on fire. It definitely wasn't the Muslims who did it." Now my question is this: When you say, "We learned," who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can just tell me the date, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday. Testimony. Yesterday, in testimony, you said, "We learned." Now, who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we, I mean those of us who were at home, me, my wife, the children. Of course no Muslim would set a mosque on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So what you're saying is here, me, my wife and my children learned that either Serb policemen or Serb soldiers had set it on fire? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: From where did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the mosque on fire. I saw it burn. And I saw when it was burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But from where did you learn that it was either Serb policemen or Serb soldiers that had set it on fire? Where did you and your wife and your children learn that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, who else could that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it was a guess, right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a guess. It's simply the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know that structures occasionally catch fire by accident, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the structure had been standing for a hundred years, and it happened to burn just then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it was an old, wooden structure, wasn't it, a hundred years old, at least, old, dry wood?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And being an electrician, you certainly know about electrical fires, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, the mosque did not have such lighting. It was an old mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you sit here and tell these Judges today, with complete certainty, that that mosque was set on fire rather than burning from other causes?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that it was a case of arson, and I can swear on my life to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But that's just a guess on your part, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are not talking about one mosque only.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. We are only talking about one mosque. We are talking about that one mosque, that's the only one we are talking about, and you're guessing, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not guessing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at a document, P898, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour do you want to take a break before I go into this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we have another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 15 or 16 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you require a break now, we'll have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Somehow I got it in my head we would break at noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Had we started at half past 10.00 we would have but we started at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This document P898, sir, you saw yesterday, I just want to draw your attention to the very first part of that document, the second paragraph. It's under the heading, "Information about the enemy." Do you see that? And then the paragraph reads, "Forces of the blue and reserve police are being mobilised in Bugojno and Donji Vakuf." Do you see that? Do you find that? It's right near the beginning?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was read to you yesterday and you were asked to confirm the presence of reserve police in Donji Vakuf. Do you remember being asked that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, they asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 50 of LiveNote, you said, your answer was, that they mobilised and armed only Serb men. That was your reaction to this, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But, sir, this document is a combat report from the 30th Partisan division in which they are providing information about the enemy. So when they talk about forces of the blue and reserve police being mobilised in Bugojno and Donji Vakuf they are talking about the mobilisation of non-Serb reserve police, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This document --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, there were no Serb men to be mobilised in Bugojno at that time, were there? It's talking about the mobilisation of Muslim forces, isn't it? Muslim police.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you think this is talking about the mobilisation of Serbs under a heading information about the enemy?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the 30th Partisan division sees Serbs as their enemy? That's your position?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was whose enemy but only they put on uniforms and armed themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all the questions I have, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I would like to ask just a few questions, Your Honour with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, this document, Mr. Doslic, that you were shown, that's your statement on 15 January, 1993. And counsel read to you this particular paragraph, if I can find it. Bear with me, Your Honour, I'm sorry, I'm trying to find it. This was the paragraph if counsel can assist me, about Krajisnik and Plavsic and the policy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's in the other document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the second statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: August.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The August statement, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The 23 August statement and it's on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This particular paragraph, which counsel referred you to in his cross-examination, within the framework or he received orders from higher levels of decision making, and were then headed by Radovan Karadzic, et cetera, may have been receiving orders and guidelines for this monstrous policy. It is these words, this monstrous policy, I want you to address the Court, please. Can you please tell us what this monstrous policy was that you were alluding to and whether you yourself was a victim of this monstrous policy.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a policy of persecution, expulsion and killing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So when you said to counsel, to this Court, that you felt it with your own skin, is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I not only felt it but also all of my neighbours and friends, many of whom disappeared, many of whom were killed, and who are not mentioned anywhere here, not a single word about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And these are your views of the matter? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here is my view point. All the inmates of all prisons were registered. We were the only one who were not registered. We were only transferred from one warehouse to another.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now can you please tell me that counsel showed you this document and I will not refer you, I think you remember it, where a Croat was -- driver was supposed to have been arrested, of the lorry, and with the coal on the bridge. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one was ever captured to date, and I don't know how much time has elapsed. No one established the truth about it. No one was ever apprehended for this crime, and I don't know who did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you ever, ever, hear about a trial having taken place in respect of this bridge?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Ilija Boroja, you said you knew him. How do you know him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had a coffee bar in town. He was a resident of our town, and I already told you it was a small place. We all knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is Boroja a very familiar name in the region? The surname Boroja.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Uniforms: Counsel asked you about the various kind of uniforms and you gave different colours, brown and blue, but is it a fact that every single person was a Serb in these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That would be all from this witness, thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have some questions for you from the Bench. The first questions will be addressed to you by Judge Janu from the Czech Republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Doslic, you said that Nikola Kisin and Nedeljko Ninkovic were your teachers. Could you please describe for the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: What sort of people they were? They were teaching you so how did you view them as a personality? Can you describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew them both as persons, as neighbours, as teachers as well, before the war they used to be normal people. They worked at school. I don't know what you would like to hear specifically. In the beginning of the 1990s, when all these events started, they joined in with the SDS, they were the greatest supporters of the SDS in Donji Vakuf, and the highest ranking officials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Before the 1990s, would you -- from the position you knew them, would you guess that they were capable of any atrocity or anything wrong, before this event?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Is it that that you concluded that they had to receive some orders because they were not capable to organise such evil what you experienced on your own skin?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing. I knew them as one kind of men before the war, and a completely different kind of men during the war. And as for Kisin, Nikola, who was a neighbour of mine from a nearby village, I liked football and I was a good player and so was he. He often came to watch our football matches and to cheer for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: But my question was, because you said they received orders, and my question was why -- because you were not witnessing that they were receiving the orders, but you logically concluded something. So my question was: Was -- because your positive experience with them, so was this the factor for your conclusion that they were themselves without the orders not capable to do anything wrong, basically wrong, what you experience later on?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly, because they were not able to drag all those units into our town, into the villages from Gradiska from other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: My second question would be more or less the same. Would you tell us about Jordan Ilic from before the war? That's first part of the question. And second part, do you know where he's living now? Did you meet him recently?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jordan Ilic lived in a certain part of town which had a majority Serb population, in a village. He worked as a carpenter at the timber factory. That's where I knew him from. During the war, however, he became a policeman. He beat people up. He provoked them, and harassed them. I saw that on more than one occasion. And I don't know the real truth of course but I hear from other people that he is dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last -- third and last question is: Would you describe for us the destruction of the mosque? You said you see the mosque -- you saw the mosque standing, and you could see the mosque burning. So just try to bring us to the picture.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we are talking about a small town where I live. Those mosques were from 100 to 300 metres apart. I don't know which mosque you mean specifically. You mean the last one mentioned or the one mentioned by this gentleman here or the one that was razed to the ground and parking was later set up there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I am discussing, or I am asking you about the mosque you discussed here with the counsel for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The first one?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Dudica mosque?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The wooden one.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I understand. That mosque was built out of wood, and solid materials. The part that goes up to the minaret was made of wood and the other part was made out of wood and solid material, half-half. It was a very old mosque, a symbol of our tradition, a very old one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: But my question was to bring us to the picture, how the destruction was going on. You said you were watching it. So did it start it slowly? When did it start, it was in the afternoon, in the night? What could you see?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it happened sometime around 10.00 or 11.00, I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly now to the hour. It was set on fire, and it burnt, emitting a dense cloud of smoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rather than a question, actually I have a little bit of a confusion in my mind resulting from two statements that you made, and one statement, the one of August, the one of August, 1994, you referred to Nedeljko Ninkovic as the President of the Donji Vakuf branch of the SDS, and then in the statement to the Prosecution of June 2001, when you refer to the events of the 22nd December, 1992, in other words when you were exchanged, and you mention the presence of Nikola Kisin, you describe him as the SDS president. Were there -- who was actually the President of the SDS in Donji Vakuf? Kisin or Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of them were there, taking turns. I don't know at what intervals, a year or two in 1990, or I don't know which year exactly it was Ninkovic and then it was Kisin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I don't have any further questions. And that means your testimony comes to an end here. You're free to go and the offices of this Tribunal will be assisting you to help you on return to your country of residence. On our part, in my own name and on behalf of also the two other Judges that sit with me in this trial, and on behalf of the Tribunal, I should like to thank you for having come over to give evidence. You will now be escorted by the usher and attended to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So ladies and gentlemen, we will have a break of 25 minutes and I take it -- will you, Madam Chana, will you be handling the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will start with the next witness, I suppose, and how long do you anticipate his -- your in chief to last, Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It's really very hard to say because I have lots of documents which I want to go over with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness is 7.194?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And there are no protective measures for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. All right. The usher presumably went to bring in the witness. All right. Tomorrow, I think you are all aware that we will be sitting in the afternoon and not in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow what I am saying in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You are about to start giving evidence in this trial that has been instituted by this Tribunal against Radoslav Brdjanin. Our rules require that before you give evidence, you enter -- you make a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth. It's the equivalent of an oath. The text of the solemn declaration is contained in a piece of paper which Madam Usher is going to hand to you. Please take that in your hand, read that statement aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us that you will be telling us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please be seated. And you're now going to be questioned first by Madam Richterova, who is appearing for the Prosecution. And she will then be followed, I don't know whether it's today, whether that will happen today or tomorrow, she will then be followed by Mr. John Ackerman, who is the lead counsel for Mr. Brdjanin. Madam Richterova, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Good afternoon. Can you please --

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: My name is Senad Alkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Doganovci, Donji Vakuf municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And when?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 1st of February, 1960.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You studied at the university of Sarajevo, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Which subject did you study?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: I studied at the school for political sciences at the national defence department.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And following the graduation, you became a high school teacher, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In 1984, you got a job with the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence in Donji Vakuf, correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was your position in 1984, assistant commander responsible for the organisation and mobilisation efforts of the TO?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And in 1989, you were promoted to commander of the TO of Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After we learn something about your background, I would like to know something about Donji Vakuf. I will show you a map of Donji Vakuf, if I can ask the usher, the map would be Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit P1692. And we can see that the Donji Vakuf municipality consists of the town of Donji Vakuf and some other villages. Can you tell us what was the ethnic composition of the Donji Vakuf municipality?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: The majority were Muslim, and then there were about 9.000 -- a little over 9.000 Serbs, 13.000 Muslims, very few Croats, 600 approximately, and the remainder of the population declared themselves as Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will show you an overview of ethnic structure in a second. Now let's stay with this map. Can you point at villages which had majority of Muslim population, please?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: The village of Torlakovac, the village of Prusac, Cehajici, Karici, Korenici, the village of Oborci, that is the central part of Oborci.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what about the town of Donji Vakuf? What was the ethnic structure within the town itself?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: I think that the Muslims were in majority with respect to the Serbs. The ratio was approximately 60 to 40 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I am done with -- I would like to show you this overview, and it is the only document which Your Honours do not have, and I just lost it. It's Exhibit P58, and it says "overview of data on the number and ethnic structure of population according to municipalities." And I will show the witness -- if the witness would be shown the page 9 of the B/C/S version? I can give you -- and you can see the name Srbobran, is it the new name for Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When was this name used for the first time, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: I think it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And according to this list, we can see, as you correctly pointed a minute ago, that there was a majority of Muslim population. It says 55 per cent, and Serbs, they had 38, and something, then we can see 1995, and it says, Muslim, 81 persons, which is 0.9 per cent of population, now only tell me very briefly, we will discuss it later, the population -- apparently the population left Donji Vakuf. When was it? When was the first wave of people leaving Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: The non-Serb population of Donji Vakuf started leaving sometime in early April, 1992. The majority of the population, however, left the town in May, around the 8th, the 9th, the 10th and the 11th of May, when they left for Travnik and Bugojno. Most of them ended up in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm done with this document. Now, we will start with the Territorial Defence. We heard that you was the commander of Territorial Defence in Donji Vakuf. Can you tell the Judges what were the main responsibilities of the TO commander?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: The responsibilities of Territorial Defence commanders or the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence included the training of the reserve forces in the Donji Vakuf municipality and mobilisation of the reserve force as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: TO, Territorial Defence, did you -- did you have in your possession weapons?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: The municipal TO had their own weapons and ammunition as well as other quartermaster equipment, which was in the possession of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And in 1990, where were the weapons stored?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: Normally, the weapons were stored, together with the ammunition, ever since these reserve units were established in the area of the Donji Vakuf municipality, in the warehouse which was located just above the MUP building in Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Maybe I can use this map. Can you recognise on this map -- and you can use my map -- if you could have a look, please, at the photo number 4, is this the building where the weapons were stored until 1990?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour we went through the process of deciding that we wouldn't put the names of the buildings on these so that the witness wouldn't be led, and then she proceeds to lead the witness by telling him exactly which one to look at and telling him what it is before he's ever asked a question about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Objection sustained. Next question, Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Next question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget about that photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we leave the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: For how long -- this -- you said the weapons were stored in TO warehouse. Were there some other places where weapons were stored, which belonged to TO?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there any weapons in companies, in factories?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: Up until 1989, a small part of the weapons were at the factories. This was later returned to the TO warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And now I would -- before I go on with the weapons in TO warehouse, tell me, were there any military facilities in Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: In Donji Vakuf, there were two facilities which were under the JNA control. One was located in Daljan and the other one in Klade. The latter had been abandoned by the JNA sometime in the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This Daljan, where was it located? Can you show us on the map?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can the witness put an X for identification of this Daljan military facility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you just mark with an X the location, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And next to that X, can I ask you to put down your initials, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, was there any time when the weapons would be moved from the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: It was not moved until the transfer to the Daljan warehouse, which occurred pursuant to an order of the district staff in Daljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And when was it? Which year it was?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was just before the elections, sometime in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In 1990, was it discussed at any meetings with your supervisors or with the district TO, whether or not to move these weapons?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: With whom did you discuss it and where?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: You couldn't really call it a discussion. The Territorial Defence district staff issued an order at a meeting held in Bugojno. The TO commander told us at the meeting that the weapons of the municipal staffs of Donji Vakuf, Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno should be relocated to the Daljan barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And this Territorial Defence district staff, when was it -- where was it? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: In Zenica, and the meeting was held at the Bugojno municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you given any reason for the transfer of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: The reason was that in case national parties should win the elections, that is the SDS, SDA or HDZ, that they would not be tempted to take these weapons and distribute them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will return to this Daljan military facility, or Daljan barracks. What was stored in this Daljan?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, ammunition and explosives and ordnance were stored in Daljan. There were very few weapons stored there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Whom this facility belonged to?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: The facility belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was there any particular unit or corps which would be in charge of these barracks?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was under the command of a Banja Luka unit, of a logistical base or something of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you happen to know who was the commander of the logistics base?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: I heard that it was Osman Selak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And who was the commander of -- in the Daljan barracks?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
utterances.text: We called him an administrator, and it was Lieutenant Darko Savic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And now to follow the weapons, you stated that the weapons were taken to Daljan barracks. How long these weapons stayed in Daljan barracks?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC
